case_facts: A ride-hailing app shared my phone number and live location with third-party advertisers without my consent, despite their privacy policy promising otherwise.

analysis.summary: A citizen alleges that a ride-hailing application disclosed their personal data — specifically phone number and live location — to third-party advertisers without obtaining consent, in direct contravention of the platform's own published privacy policy. This raises issues of data privacy violation, breach of contract, and unfair trade practice under consumer protection law. The matter potentially engages both the Information Technology Act framework and the Consumer Protection Act.

transcript.speaker: ai
transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, I appear on behalf of the Complainant, a consumer who placed her trust — and her personal safety — in the hands of the Respondent ride-hailing company, only to have that trust shattered by a deliberate, undisclosed sharing of her phone number and live location data with third-party advertisers. This is not a technical breach of a fine-print clause. This is a fundamental violation of a constitutionally protected right.

Your Lordship, the Supreme Court in **K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India** (docid: 1199182) — speaking through a nine-judge bench, the highest constitutional authority this nation possesses — held unequivocally that informational privacy is a facet of the right to life and personal liberty under **Article 21**, and that any processing of personal data must satisfy the twin pillars of **consent and purpose limitation**. The Respondent's own privacy policy promised that data would not be shared with third parties. That promise was the consent architecture. The moment the Respondent shared live location and phone numbers with advertisers — entities entirely outside the stated purpose of providing transportation — they shattered both pillars simultaneously. There was no consent; there was no legitimate purpose. The constitutional violation is complete on the face of the record.

Your Lordship, the Respondent is not a passive actor here. It is a sophisticated commercial enterprise that actively harvested sensitive personal data — real-time geolocation, no less — as a condition of service, and then monetised it covertly. A consumer's live location is not merely commercial metadata; it is a roadmap to her physical whereabouts at every moment. The potential for stalking, harassment, and physical harm is self-evident. This Court must recognise that where a private entity makes a binding representation in its privacy policy and then acts in direct contradiction to it, it assumes absolute accountability for the consequences. The principle articulated in **Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan** (docid: 4087220) is instructive: where a positive duty exists — here, the duty to protect data as promised — and that duty is breached, this Court has both the authority and the obligation to impose binding remedial obligations, even in the absence of comprehensive statutory codification of data protection law.

Your Lordship, I therefore submit that the Complainant is entitled to: (i) a declaration that the Respondent violated her fundamental right to informational privacy under **Article 21**; (ii) compensatory damages for the distress, loss of autonomy, and exposure to risk caused by this breach; and (iii) a direction to the Respondent to immediately cease all such data-sharing practices and submit to an independent audit. The Respondent cannot hide behind corporate opacity. This Court must send an unambiguous message that personal data shared in confidence is not a commodity to be traded in the shadows.
